title: One new thing at a time
keyIdea: Your thinking space can only juggle a few new things at once. When a task feels like too much, count what is new, keep the thing you are learning new, and make everything else easy and known. Add the next new thing only when the first one is right and easy, not just right once.
familyTip: When homework or a hobby feels like too much, ask: “What is new here?” Count the new things together. Pick the one that matters most and make the rest easy: smaller numbers, no timer, a book on a topic they know. When the new part feels easy, ask: “What new thing shall we add next?”

visual.caption: One new thing, or too much new at once? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A new spelling rule, using words you can already read
A new maths method with huge numbers and a timer
A new swimming stroke in the shallow end
A new song and a new dance to it, both on day one
The new 8 times table, with no timer at first
Your first time cooking alone, with a new recipe

lab.caption: Flagship lab: spot what is new on Kai’s page, strip it back to one new thing, flag the day he is ready, build Mo’s piano stairs, then sort plans.

kid: Your brain has a small thinking space for new things. It can only juggle a few at once. Things you know well take up almost no room. New things take up lots of room.

Kai is learning to take away by swapping a ten for ten ones. His page also has big numbers and long word stories. That is 3 new things at once. His thinking space is full, so he makes slips and gets stuck.
So Kai keeps one thing new: the swap. He uses small numbers he knows and plain sums. Now he has room to think about the swap, and he gets them right.

When is he ready for the next new thing? Not the first time he gets them all right. He waits until they are right and easy, with no hard thinking. Then he adds big numbers. One new thing, then the next, then the next.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. Working memory can hold and work on only a few new elements at once, while knowledge already stored in long-term memory costs very little (cognitive load theory: Sweller 1988; Sweller, van Merriënboer and Paas 2019). When several new elements interact, as in a new method with unfamiliar numbers and a wordy context, the load can swamp a learner. Teaching the parts on their own first and combining them later helps (Pollock, Chandler and Sweller 2002), as does presenting new material in small steps with practice after each (Rosenshine 2012).

Fluency matters for the next step: once a skill is automatic it needs little attention, which frees room for the next new element (LaBerge and Samuels 1974). The lab makes this concrete. The learner counts the new parts of a page, turns the non-goal parts back to known, picks the day a skill is right and easy, builds a piano practice plan one stair at a time, and sorts plans.

Common mistakes: thinking more new things at once means faster learning; treating one perfect but slow score as ready; making the goal itself easier instead of the parts around it; jumping two steps at once; and staying on the easy step for ever. Be careful with the lab's three thinking slots and its Try 5 scores: they are a picture of the idea, not a measure of real working memory. Reducing load is for learning something new; it is not a reason to keep work easy once it is fluent.

Related lessons: Chunking to remember groups items so they take less room; Breaking tasks into steps splits a job into parts; Deliberate practice targets weak spots. This lesson is about how much is new at once and when to add the next new thing.

practice.prompt: A page has a new method, new big numbers and a timer. How many new things is that?
practice.hint: Count each part that the learner has never done before.
practice.explain: 3: the method, the big numbers and the timer are all new. That is too much at once.

practice.prompt: A practice page has {a} new things on it. You want only 1 new thing. How many must you change back to something known?
practice.hint: Keep the one you are learning. Every other new thing must go back to known.
practice.explain: {a} take away the 1 you keep is {=a-1}. Change {=a-1} things back to known.

practice.prompt: Ana gets all her new 6 times table right, but slowly. What should she do next?
choices: Keep practising until it is easy
Add a timer and 7s and 8s now
Stop, she has learned it
practice.hint: Ready means two things. Which one is missing?
practice.explain: Keep practising until it is easy. Right but slow still takes all her thinking space.

practice.prompt: Mo adds one new thing on each stair of his piano plan. He starts with one hand on stair 1. How many new things has he added by stair {n}?
practice.hint: One new thing per stair. Count the stairs up to {n}.
practice.explain: One new thing on each of {n} stairs makes {n} new things, one at a time.

practice.prompt: Lee is learning long division. Which part should stay new?
choices: The long division method
Huge new numbers
A new timer
practice.hint: What is Lee actually trying to learn?
practice.explain: The long division method stays new. Use numbers he knows and no timer.

pool.prompt: Why does a page with lots of new things feel too hard?
choices: The new things fill your small thinking space
You are not clever enough
New things are always bad
pool.hint: Think of Kai’s thinking slots in the lab.
pool.explain: New things fill your small thinking space, so there is no room left to think.

pool.prompt: Which plan has just one new thing?
choices: A new swimming stroke in the shallow end
A new stroke in the deep end, in a race
A new stroke, a new pool and a new coach
pool.hint: Count what is new in each plan.
pool.explain: In the shallow end only the stroke is new, so all your thinking can go on it.

pool.prompt: When are you ready to add the next new thing?
choices: When the first one is right and easy
The first time you get one right
Never, stay where it is easy
pool.hint: Right once is not the same as right and easy.
pool.explain: When it is right and easy, it needs little thinking, so there is room for the next new thing.

pool.prompt: Jo says, “Easy numbers are for babies. I will learn the new method with huge numbers.” What is the slip?
choices: Easy numbers leave room to learn the method
Huge numbers make the method easier
There is no slip
pool.hint: What happens to the thinking space with two new things?
pool.explain: Easy numbers are not babyish. They leave room in the thinking space for the new method.

pool.prompt: Mo can play the right hand alone, slowly. What is the best next stair?
choices: Left hand alone, slowly
Both hands at full speed
A whole new tune
pool.hint: Which choice adds only one new thing?
pool.explain: Left hand alone, slowly adds one new thing. Full speed with both hands adds several.

pool.prompt: Kai does {n} sums a day for {d} days before he adds the next new thing. How many sums is that?
pool.hint: {n} sums each day, for {d} days. Multiply.
pool.explain: {n} times {d} is {=n*d} sums of practice before the next new thing.

pool.prompt: A new card game feels like too much. What could help?
choices: Learn one rule first, with cards you know
Learn all 12 rules at once
Never play it
pool.hint: Cut what is new. Do not give up.
pool.explain: Learn one rule first. When it is easy, add the next rule.

pool.prompt: A plan adds one new thing each week. How many weeks to add {n} new things?
pool.hint: One new thing per week. How many weeks for {n}?
pool.explain: {n} new things at one a week takes {n} weeks, and each one gets easy before the next.
